messages.content:
Read this scene from a novel and say what it tells us about time. Don't work out a day number: only what the text says.

## End of the Previous Scene

and patted children on the head, and questioned beggars, and looked down into the kitchens of houses, and up to the windows, and found that everything could yield him pleasure. He had never dreamed that any walk--that anything--could give him so much happiness. In the afternoon he turned his steps towards his nephew's house. He passed the door a dozen times, before he had the courage to go up and knock. But he made a dash, and did it: "Is your master at home, my dear?" said Scrooge to the girl. Nice girl! Very. "Yes, sir." "Where is he, my love?" said Scrooge. "He's in the dining-room, sir, along with mistress. I'll show you up-stairs, if you please." "Thank'ee. He knows me," said Scrooge, with his hand already on the dining-room lock. "I'll go in here, my dear." He turned it gently, and sidled his face in, round the door. They were looking at the table (which was spread out in great array); for these young housekeepers are always nervous on such points, and like to see that everything is right. "Fred!" said Scrooge. Dear heart alive, how his niece by marriage started! Scrooge had forgotten, for the moment, about her sitting in the corner with the footstool, or he wouldn't have done it, on any account. "Why bless my soul!" cried Fred, "who's that?" "It's I. Your uncle Scrooge. I have come to dinner. Will you let me in, Fred?" Let him in! It is a mercy he didn't shake his arm off. He was at home in five minutes. Nothing could be heartier. His niece looked just the same. So did Topper when he came. So did the plump sister when she came. So did every one when they came. Wonderful party, wonderful games, wonderful unanimity, won-der-ful happiness!

## Scene: scrooge-raises-bobs-salary

But he was early at the office next morning. Oh, he was early there. If he could only be there first, and catch Bob Cratchit coming late! That was the thing he had set his heart upon.

And he did it; yes, he did! The clock struck nine. No Bob. A quarter past. No Bob. He was full eighteen minutes and a half behind his time. Scrooge sat with his door wide open, that he might see him come into the Tank.

His hat was off, before he opened the door; his comforter too. He was on his stool in a jiffy; driving away with his pen, as if he were trying to overtake nine o'clock.

"Hallo!" growled Scrooge, in his accustomed voice, as near as he could feign it. "What do you mean by coming here at this time of day?"

"But you gave me the whole of to-day as well, sir," said Bob. "You said I need not come in till the twenty-seventh."

"You are?" repeated Scrooge. "Yes. I think you are. Step this way, sir, if you please."

"It's only once a year, sir," pleaded Bob, appearing from the Tank. "It shall not be repeated. I was making rather merry yesterday, sir."

"Now, I'll tell you what, my friend," said Scrooge, "I am not going to stand this sort of thing any longer. And therefore," he continued, leaping from his stool, and giving Bob such a dig in the waistcoat that he staggered back into the Tank again; "and therefore I am about to raise your salary!"

Bob trembled, and got a little nearer to the ruler. He had a momentary idea of knocking Scrooge down with it, holding him, and calling to the people in the court for help and a strait-waistcoat.

"A merry Christmas, Bob!" said Scrooge, with an earnestness that could not be mistaken, as he clapped him on the back. "A merrier Christmas, Bob, my good fellow, than I have given you, for many a year! I'll raise your salary, and endeavour to assist your struggling family, and we will discuss your affairs this very afternoon, over a Christmas bowl of smoking bishop, Bob! Make up the fires, and buy another coal-scuttle before you dot another i, Bob Cratchit!"

Scrooge was better than his word. He did it all, and infinitely more; and to Tiny Tim, who did NOT die, he was a second father. He became as good a friend, as good a master, and as good a man, as the good old city knew, or any other good old city, town, or borough, in the good old world. Some people laughed to see the alteration in him, but he let them laugh, and little heeded them; for he was wise enough to know that nothing ever happened on this globe, for good, at which some people did not have their fill of laughter in the outset; and knowing that such as these would be blind anyway, he thought it quite as well that they should wrinkle up their eyes in grins, as have the malady in less attractive forms. His own heart laughed: and that was quite enough for him.

He had no further intercourse with Spirits, but lived upon the Total Abstinence Principle, ever afterwards; and it was always said of him, that he knew how to keep Christmas well, if any man alive possessed the knowledge. May that be truly said of us, and all of us! And so, as Tiny Tim observed, God bless Us, Every One!


## Instructions

Output each field on its own labeled line.

TIME_RELATION: [when this scene happens relative to the scene before it in reading order — one of: continues (picks up at the same time or moments later), later (some time after it), earlier (before it: a flashback or a recollection told as a scene, including a past that a spirit, dream or vision shows a character; also a scene whose present is only a line or a short lead-in before it mostly tells the past, such as a story a character tells or the narrator's account of someone's youth, but not one where the present has real action on the page around the telling), frame (narration from after the story, looking back), vision (events that have not happened, or may not happen, as the story tells them: a prophecy, a future a character is shown that may be averted, a dream of what might come; the past is always earlier, even when a spirit, a dream or a vision shows it), unclear]
TIME_GAP: [the gap from the previous scene in at most six words, no explanation: "an hour", "the next morning", "three weeks", "five years", "several weeks"; empty if none is stated or implied]
TIME_ANCHOR: [a calendar fact pinning when THIS scene's action happens — a date, weekday, month, season, holiday or named day ("the hottest day of the summer") — quoted briefly; not a habit ("every Friday") or a date the scene only mentions; empty if none]
TIME_REFERS: [any statement in this scene of how long ago or how long until another event in the story, quoted briefly: "that June night three months before", "five years since he'd seen her", "the funeral was on the third day"; separate several with semicolons; empty if none]
TIME_SPAN: [when the scene summarizes a stretch of time ("all that summer"), how long; empty for a scene that plays out in one sitting]
TIME_DATE: [only what this scene's own text states about the calendar date, in EDTF: "1922-07-04", "XXXX-07-04" when the year isn't given here, "1922" for a year, "1922-22" for summer 1922 (21 spring, 22 summer, 23 autumn, 24 winter), "1917~" for "around 1917", "1922-06/1922-09" for a stretch. A date the text fixes by a stated distance from a named calendar day counts as given, marked ~: "In two weeks it'll be the longest day in the year" → "XXXX-06-07~". Never fill in a part the text doesn't give; empty if the text gives no date]

TIME_RELATION: later

TIME_GAP: the next morning

TIME_ANCHOR: "the twenty-seventh"

TIME_REFERS: "the whole of to-day as well"; "I have given you, for many a year"

TIME_SPAN: His subsequent life ("ever afterwards")

TIME_DATE: XXXX-12-26~
